name: Root work and Gullah herbal remedies
what_people_do: Families in the South and Sea Islands use teas, poultices and spiritual practice drawn from herbal lore; the tradition is documented in books.
why_they_say_it_works: Remedies handed down from enslaved ancestors; belief that plants and spiritual work treat illness.

documented_by.source: Mitchell F, Hoodoo Medicine: Gullah Herbal Remedies (1978; reissued 1999); Lee ME, Working the Roots; Covey HC, African American Slave Medicine (2007); Fontenot WL, Secret Doctors (1994). Titles and dates from library records via agent4; NOT opened this session
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Four ethnographic and documentary books (Mitchell, Lee, Covey, Fontenot) on Gullah, root work and African American slave medicine. Agent4 confirmed their existence via library records; I did not open them or extract specific practices.

evidence.finding: My search found no peer-reviewed pharmacological or clinical testing of these plants as a body of remedies. A herbal-school blog says at least 76 species are documented from the Sea Islands (UNVERIFIED).

source.name: agent4-traditional-practices.md, 12 Nov 2026 (research file in this project)

harm_note: Unknown: no individual plant or recipe examined.
gaps: Specific remedies not extracted; books not read.
